title: How Tupperware Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the history of Tupperware, from inventor Earl Tupper's ambitious, tinkering youth and his polyethylene bowls with the burping seal, through Brownie Wise's hostess party sales model, the Jubilee company parties, Tupper's firing of Wise and sale of the company, later redesigns and modern party culture including drag Tupperware shows. The episode closes with listener mail about the Streisand effect.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and burping containers
segments.summary: The hosts joke about whether a Tupperware burp is a real burp and compare the seal's sound to cartoons, then tease the topic of Tupperware.

segments.title: Earl Tupper's early life and inventions
segments.summary: Earl Tupper is introduced as an ambitious, grouchy tinkerer who clashed with his father, and who had a book of inventions that mostly failed to catch on, such as a better stocking garter and customized cigarettes.

segments.title: Tupper's tree doctor business and plastics work at Vistalloid
segments.summary: Tupper's tree doctoring business failed during the Depression, and he went to work for the Vistalloid plant, a DuPont division, in a Massachusetts town known for plastics experimentation. He developed molding methods for polyethylene.

segments.title: Design of the burping seal and early Tupperware bowls
segments.summary: Tupper drew the airtight seal idea from paint can lids and created the Wonder Bowl. The seal preserved food, which mattered to homemakers who had lived through the Depression. The hosts compare the product to cheap modern knockoffs and note the company's lifetime guarantee.

segments.title: Early sales struggles and Brownie Wise's hostess party model
segments.summary: Tupperware sold poorly in department and hardware stores. Brownie Wise, a Stanley Home Products salesperson who had started her own Tupperware Patio Parties company, began selling through in-home demonstration parties. Her company was later hired by Tupper.

segments.title: Brownie Wise builds the sales army and the Jubilee
segments.summary: Wise divided the company between Massachusetts manufacturing and Orlando home sales, and built a tiered sales hierarchy of consultants, managers and distributors. She noticed suburban women were bored and looked for work. The annual Jubilee company party included buried prizes.

segments.title: Growth of Tupperware worldwide and modern markets
segments.summary: The hosts describe Tupperware's global party reach, with most sales now outside the US, and the company's China water filter sales. They discuss the decline of Wise's later life and the hosts' brief speculation about her fate.

segments.title: Tupper fires Brownie Wise and sells the company
segments.summary: Tupper grew jealous of Wise's celebrity and fired her with one year's salary and no stock. He then pressed her about company spending in Florida. She started Cinderella Cosmetics, which folded. Tupper sold the company for about sixteen million dollars in 1958, then moved to Costa Rica.

segments.title: Tupperware design legacy and later redesign
segments.summary: The original Millionaire line came in six colors and remains collectible. Tupper refused to design pet bowls. Designer Morrison Cousins redesigned the line for older users with flap-style seals and contrasting lids, and brought the brand online. The hosts mention an early-nineties live home shopping broadcast.

segments.title: Tupperware drag parties and documentary
segments.summary: The hosts discuss drag performer Dixie Longate, who sells Tupperware in drag shows, and a drag queen named Aunt Barbara who was a top North American seller. They mention a PBS documentary about Tupperware.

segments.title: Listener mail: the Streisand effect
segments.summary: A listener explains the Streisand effect, using the 2003 lawsuit over a photo of Barbra Streisand's Malibu home, which drew far more attention after the suit became news.
